nameStory: The Minute Jumping Spider earned its name from its incredibly tiny size - even smaller than most of its already petite jumping spider cousins. At just a few millimeters long, this little acrobat is so small that 'minute' (pronounced my-NOOT, meaning extremely small) perfectly captures just how easy it is to overlook this miniature marvel.
description: The Minute Jumping Spider is one of New England's tiniest jumping spiders, measuring only 2-3 millimeters in length - about the size of a pencil tip. Like all jumping spiders, it has a compact, robust body with relatively short legs and those characteristic large front eyes that give it excellent vision for hunting. This little spider is typically dark brown to black with subtle lighter markings, though you'll need a magnifying glass to appreciate the details. Despite its diminutive size, it's an active hunter that stalks prey with the same athletic prowess as its larger jumping spider relatives.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small at just 2-3mm long - smaller than a peppercorn and easily mistaken for a speck of dirt until it moves

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large front-facing eyes arranged in a square pattern, giving it an almost cartoon-like face when viewed with magnification

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and chunky build typical of jumping spiders, with a relatively flat, oval abdomen and sturdy-looking legs

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Dark brown to blackish coloration with faint lighter patterns that may appear as subtle stripes or spots under magnification

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with frequent stops, often turning to face you directly when disturbed due to their excellent vision

habitat: Look for Minute Jumping Spiders in sunny, open areas with low vegetation like meadows, field edges, and garden borders. They're often found hunting on flowers, leaves, and stems of herbaceous plants where their tiny prey congregates. These spiders prefer warm, exposed locations where they can bask in sunlight while actively hunting for small insects and mites.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning their hunting season on emerging vegetation and early flowers.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most easily spotted hunting during warm, sunny days. Mating and egg-laying occur during this season.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, but adults begin to decline as temperatures drop and prey becomes scarce.
seasonality.winter: Likely overwinters as eggs or immature spiders in protected locations, with adults rarely seen during cold months.

funFact: Despite being so small you could fit dozens on a dime, Minute Jumping Spiders have vision that's proportionally better than many animals hundreds of times their size - they can spot and track prey from distances that would be equivalent to a human clearly seeing a basketball from over a mile away!
confusionNotes: Most commonly mistaken for tiny bits of debris or other minute spiders, but the characteristic jumping spider behavior of stopping, turning to face observers, and making quick directional movements helps distinguish it from similarly-sized spiders that move more smoothly.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name 'Talavera' refers to a type of colorful Mexican pottery, though this particular species is quite subdued in coloration compared to some of its more vibrant international relatives. The scientific name reflects both the pottery connection and the spider's tiny stature.
compareHints: Since this is the only Talavera species in New England, compare it to other tiny jumping spiders in the region. The Minute Jumping Spider is generally smaller than most other jumping spiders and lacks the bright colors or bold patterns seen in species like the Bold Jumping Spider or Paradise Jumping Spider. Its uniformly dark coloration and exceptionally small size make it distinctive among the jumping spider family.
